{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "Teodor kept the lighthouse the way his mother had kept it, which is to say he lit the lamp at dusk whether or not a ship was due, and he did not tell visitors why the beam swept twice fast and once slow. The pattern was older than his family's tenure. He had wound the clockwork, by his own rough estimate, some fifteen thousand evenings, and he had stopped estimating because the number had begun to sound less like devotion and more like a sentence.

A woman climbed the path on the last clear night of autumn with boots wrong for the rocks and a notebook she never opened. She stood at the base of the tower rather than coming inside, which told him most of what he needed to know.

"Is this the light for the strait?"

"It's the only light."

"I meant—does anyone ever wreck here anyway?"

Teodor checked the oil and struck the wick. He had learned that people asked about wrecks when they were carrying one, and asked whether it was the only light when they wanted permission to stop looking for another.

"Same rocks," he said. "Different weather."

She laughed without much in it and pulled her collar up. Near midnight the fog came in from the west and the beam went soft and wide, the way it always did. She shivered.

"Does it always do that?"

"Every fog. Same hour."

"Then you'd think you'd stop worrying."

"You'd think." He adjusted the lens. "But I want to worry. The night the fog feels harmless is the night I stop climbing the stairs."

Far out, a green running light blinked and held. She didn't move toward the path.

"Dawn's at six," he said. "You don't have to go down yet."

"When do I have to?"

"At six," said Teodor. "That's what the light is for.""}
